title: The force of imagination
hook: imagination can make us ill or well (Essays 1.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, different roads: sometimes pity softens a conqueror, sometimes courage. Your line was different roads. Did you try the road you usually skip? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

A passenger on a plane starts scratching their head. Two minutes later, the passenger behind them is scratching too. Nothing has landed on that second head. Nothing has changed except a picture in a mind. Or someone at a dinner party describes, in detail, a dentist's drill, and around the table, jaws start to clench. Montaigne noticed this in himself and gave it an essay, which opens on a Latin saying of the scholars: a strong imagination produces the event.
screen: `AN ITCH ON A PLANE.` → `THE ROW BEHIND STARTS TOO.` → `A PICTURE DID THAT.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. Montaigne says plainly that he's one of the people imagination works on hardest. The sight of someone else's pain gives him a pain of his own. A man who keeps coughing near him makes his own lungs and throat feel raw. He doesn't tell this as a theory. He tells it as a report on his body. Second, the pin. He tells of a woman who was sure she'd swallowed a pin with her bread, and cried out that she could feel it stuck in her throat. Someone sensible guessed it was her imagination, made her throw up, and slipped a bent pin into what came up. Seeing it, she felt her pain lift. Third, the doctors. Montaigne notes that physicians work on a patient's imagination too, winning their belief with promises of a cure, so that imagination can do part of the work. Imagination, in this essay, can make us ill, and it can help make us well. Fourth, his honesty about his stories. Montaigne admits he can't vouch for every tale he borrows. He leaves them on the conscience of whoever told them. What matters to him is that they're possible, and that they show something true about how people are made. That's a careful line for a writer to draw, and it fits the subject: he's an author who knows his own mind can run ahead of the facts. In a plain week, the force of imagination is the email you've decided is angry before you open it, or the knock on the door that sounds like bad news. Montaigne's move is to notice it: the mind is making a picture, and the body is believing it.
screen: `HE FEELS OTHERS' PAIN.` · `A WOMAN AND A BENT PIN.` · `DOCTORS WORK ON BELIEF.` · `HE LEAVES TALES TO THEIR TELLERS.` · then, large: `IT IMAGINES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice imagination at work. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Now try a small test. Bring to mind a lemon: yellow, cold from the fridge, cut in half, juice on the board. Notice what your mouth does. Let it go. Then bring to mind something you've been dreading this week, and notice what your shoulders, stomach, or jaw do. Nothing in the room changed. Each time you notice it, name it quietly: it imagines. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The force of imagination. Montaigne's essay on how a picture in the mind can stir pain or ease in the body, starting with his own. Today's word.
Your line: it imagines. Today, when your body tightens over something that hasn't happened, say it imagines, and check what's actually in front of you. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne turn to his essay on the force of imagination for its frank self-report: he describes how pictures in his own mind stir pain or relief in his body, and how others use that power.

fork.setup: a woman is sure she swallowed a pin and feels it in her throat. you suspect it's her imagination. what does the person in Montaigne's story do?
options: tell her firmly she's imagining it.
make her throw up and slip a bent pin into what comes up.
ignore her until she calms down.
fork.reveal: the pain lifted when she saw the pin. Montaigne tells it to show that what the mind believes, the body can feel.

original.note: Latin: a strong imagination produces the event, the saying Montaigne opens this essay with.

trapdoor: what you thought: the force of imagination is about creativity.
what it means: a picture in the mind can stir real pain or relief in the body, and Montaigne starts with his own.
what a scholar hears: Montaigne opens on a Latin tag and closes by admitting he can't vouch for every story he borrows, only that they're possible.

sources.ref: Essays 1.21, Of the force of imagination (the Latin tag; his own susceptibility; another's cough; the woman and the pin; physicians and the patient's imagination; borrowed stories left to their authors)

notes: Chapter numbering: this essay is 1.21 in the path's outline (and in Villey's French edition); some English editions (Cotton/Hazlitt) number it 1.20. Confirm.
The pin story and the passage on leaving borrowed tales on the conscience of their tellers are paraphrased from memory of the essay; confirm both are in this chapter.
Latin tag 'Fortis imaginatio generat casum' ('say the scholars', in Montaigne); confirm wording and the pronunciation guide (ecclesiastical vs classical).
The practice uses the lemon exercise and a mild 'dread' check; no health claims are made. Montaigne's own claims about illness and cure are given as his, not as medical advice.

Editor: the Latin line is the essay's opening sentence (a saying of the scholars), not a heading; the physicians line now follows Montaigne's own, more pointed account (promises of cure working through belief); varied the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn.
